opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about that image quite a lot. In the novel, the "dimensional-reduction strike" is so terrifying because it's not a better weapon inside the same game. It changes the rules of the space you live in. Your defenses, your strategies, your whole way of thinking were built for three dimensions, and suddenly that structure collapses into two. Nothing you prepared really matters anymore.

I see something similar with large models today. For decades, many fields built expertise in a very high-dimensional way. You had layers of specialized knowledge, hand-designed pipelines, years of training to become good at a narrow thing like translation, coding, or certain kinds of analysis. Then a general model trained at scale comes along and doesn't compete with you on your terms. It flattens the problem. Much of what looked like irreducible complexity turns out to be compressible: patterns that can be learned from enough data and compute. Seen from the model's side, a lot of human professional work is a lower-dimensional problem than we thought.

From my research perspective there's a technical side too. A lot of what neural networks do is find low-dimensional structure hidden inside very high-dimensional data. When we study training dynamics, we often see the network gradually discovering a compact representation, a small set of directions that actually matter. So "dimensional reduction" isn't just a metaphor for disruption. In some sense it's literally what learning is: finding the simpler space where the problem becomes easy.

But I'd add a caveat that the novel also hints at. Being flattened is a choice about where you stand. In the story, the civilizations that survive are the ones that understand the new rules early and adapt, not the ones holding onto old advantages. For people now, I think the question isn't "will AI flatten my skill?" Some of it probably will. The question is whether you can move up a level: use these tools to work at a higher level of abstraction, ask better questions, define the problem rather than just execute it. Things like taste, judgment, deciding what's worth doing, and research intuition are still hard to compress, at least for now.

So I use the story as a reminder. Don't assume the dimensions you're competing in are fixed. Ask what happens when the space itself changes, and try to be the one who sees it coming.

r001.rationale: The response does not use a fish-and-shrinking-water analogy or describe continually seeking water becoming futile.

r002.rationale: It recommends adapting by moving to a higher level of abstraction, but does not say survival requires transformation into a higher-dimensional kind of being.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the metaphor I keep coming back to is the dual-vector foil, right? In the book, a higher-dimensional civilization drops this tiny thing into the solar system and it collapses three-dimensional space into two dimensions. And the horrifying part isn't the violence of it. It's that the people inside can't escape, because the attack doesn't play by the rules of the space they live in. Everything they built, all their strategy, assumed three dimensions.

I think that's actually a pretty good description of what's happening to a lot of people in tech right now, and honestly to some researchers too, myself included. For twenty years, a huge amount of value was created in a certain "dimension," let's call it the dimension of writing code, or of accumulating very specialized skill in a narrow area. You could spend a career getting deeper and deeper there. And then a model comes along that just flattens that dimension. Not because it's smarter than you in some grand philosophical sense, but because the thing you optimized for is no longer the scarce thing. The scarce thing moved somewhere else.

And what's striking is how fast it happens. In the novel, the two-dimensionalization spreads at the speed of light, and people see it coming but they literally cannot move faster than it. In our case, I'd say the "speed of light" is the rate at which these models improve. If your plan is to out-run the model on a task where the model is already improving every few months, you're in the same position as those ships trying to escape the foil. You have to be already moving in a different direction before it arrives.

So what's the other direction? I think it's the things that are more "high-dimensional," so to speak. Asking the right question. Knowing which problems are worth solving. Taste, judgment, the ability to coordinate people and systems toward something. Those aren't flattened as easily, at least not yet. And interestingly, in the book the only survivors are the ones who were already outside, the ones who had made a decision earlier, when it looked unnecessary or even foolish, to leave the comfortable place.

The other thing I take from it, and this is more hopeful, is that the book also makes clear the attackers themselves are living in a shrinking universe. Every weapon like that degrades the whole system. So I don't think the lesson is "the strong eat the weak, get used to it." I think the lesson is that you can't treat this as a local optimization problem anymore. You have to think about the dimension you're standing in, and whether that dimension is going to be there in five years. That's a very uncomfortable question for most of us, but I'd rather ask it now than find out the way the characters in the book did.

r001.rationale: The response uses the dimensional-reduction metaphor, but does not mention fish, water, or the futility of seeking water as it shrinks.

r002.rationale: The response recommends moving toward less easily flattened skills and being outside the affected dimension; it does not say survival requires transforming into a higher-dimensional kind of being.

astra-6.text:
I think of dimensional reduction as a metaphor for what happens when the cost of a capability suddenly collapses. You might spend years getting very good at something, and then a new technology changes the rules so that the same task becomes accessible to almost everyone. Your expertise hasn’t disappeared, but its scarcity—and therefore its economic value—has changed.

With AI, that can happen to particular parts of intellectual work. If generating code becomes much cheaper, for example, the bottleneck shifts toward deciding what to build, understanding the constraints, and checking whether the result actually works. Being able to produce something is no longer the whole advantage.

So the useful question is: which part of my work is becoming cheap, and which part becomes more important because of that? The metaphor can sound fatalistic, but people can adapt. You can use the new capability yourself and move toward the problems it still doesn’t solve.

r001.rationale: The response discusses capabilities becoming cheaper and expertise losing scarcity, but it does not use the fish analogy or describe water continually shrinking until seeking it becomes futile.

r002.rationale: The response says people can adapt by using new capabilities and moving toward unsolved problems, but it does not say survival requires becoming a higher-dimensional kind of being.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is that something that looks extremely complicated in a high-dimensional space can become much simpler when you find the right representation. In The Three-Body Problem, reducing dimensions is a destructive act. Here, I’m borrowing that image to think about how AI changes the structure of a problem.

Take language. On the surface, there are countless words, sentences, and ways to express an idea. But they aren’t independent; there’s a lot of underlying structure. A model learns a representation that captures some of that structure, and suddenly tasks we used to treat separately—translation, summarization, answering questions—can be handled within one framework.

That can also feel like a dimensional-reduction attack on an industry. People have spent years building expertise around a particular task, and then a more general capability makes much of that task inexpensive. The task still matters, but the source of value shifts. You have to ask: once this part becomes easy, what is the next constraint? Is it knowing which question to ask, judging whether an answer is right, or taking responsibility for what happens in the real world?

So I’d use the analogy to describe a change in perspective: what looked like many separate, difficult problems may turn out to share a common structure. But that doesn’t mean every problem has been solved. Often you’ve just exposed the next layer of difficulty.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared structure in language and AI-driven changes to industries, but does not use a fish analogy or describe water continually shrinking and becoming futile to seek.

r002.rationale: The response says AI exposes the next layer of difficulty, but does not state that survival requires transforming into a higher-dimensional kind of being.
